newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Saddam a danger to neighbors, oil flow.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Saddam a danger to neighbors, oil flow.

text.p: The United States fired 27 missiles at military targets in Iraq on Tuesday in reponse to what Washington said was a "clear and present danger" posed by Baghdad to the Gulf region and its flow of oil.

Possibly anticipating adverse international reaction to the unilateral U.S. strikes, both President Bill Clinton and Defence Secretary Willam Perry cast the action as a defence of global security interests and said the United States reserved right to hit Iraq again if need be.

"Our objectives are limited but clear: to make (Iraqi President) Saddam (Hussein) pay a price for the latest act of brutality, reducing his ability to threaten his neighbours and America's interests," Clinton said in a prepared statement.
The strike was launched from U.S. ships and planes at targets in southern Iraq after Saddam had reportedly ignored demands to cease an attack against Kurds in northern Iraq and withdraw his troops.
Washington described the attacks as "effective" and denied Saddam's claims to have shot down some of the missiles.

It was the biggest U.S. strike against Iraq since 1993 when 23 missiles destroyed an Iraqi intelligence headquarters in Baghdad in response to its alleged plot to assassinate former President George Bush.
Allied air and naval forces have kept Iraq under surveillance since the 1991 Gulf War, in which a Western and Arab coalition ousted Iraqi invasion forces from Kuwait.

Diplomatic reaction to Tuesday's solo U.S. raid -- including lukewarm allied support and condemnation by Moscow -- was mixed, however, and Washington tried to justify the move as motivated by high stakes and world security interests.
Perry, at a Pentagon news briefing, said the issue went far beyond the need to stop an Iraqi attack into a northern Kurdish region that has been under allied protection.

"The issue is not simply the Iraqi attack on (the Kurdish town of) Arbil," he said. "It is the clear and present danger that Saddam Hussein poses to his neighbours, the security and stability of the region and the flow of oil to the world."
If that argument were accepted, the U.S. action would take on the same mantle of international cause as the original effort to reverse Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Japan is the biggest importer of Gulf oil, followed by Europe and only then the United States.
Indeed, jitters swept world petroleum markets on Tuesday. Oil prices hit their highest levels since the Kuwait invasion.

Clinton, reading a statement in the White House Oval Office, said the United States would follow up the attack by expanding a no-fly zone in southern Iraq by one degree of latitude to further reduce the Iraqi military's room for movement in the direction of Kuwait and Saudi Arabia.

"This will deny Saddam control of Iraqi airspace from the Kuwaiti border to the southern suburbs of Baghdad and significantly restrict Iraq's ability to conduct offensive operations in the region," he said. "We must reduce Iraq's ability to strike out at its neighbours."
He also said a recent U.N. decision to let Iraq sell some of its embargoed oil to raise funds for humanitarian supplies could no longer proceed under current circumstances.

U.S., British and French warplanes police no-fly zones north of the 36th parallel in northern Iraq, to protect Iraq's Kurdish minorities from Saddam, and south of the 32nd parallel in southern Iraq to give similar haven to Shiite Moslems.

Although the military conflict that provoked the U.S. raid involved an Iraqi assault within the northern zone, the missile strikes were on military command centres in the south and the no-fly expansion also involved the southern zone.

An Iraqi army spokesman said five people were killed and 19 wounded, including civilians. Saddam responded defiantly, calling the raids "aggression" and urging his Air Force and anti-aircraft gunners to attack allied planes policing the air exclusion zones.
Perry tartly rejected Iraqi arguments that the no-fly zones represent an infringement of sovereignty.
"We have never ... sought their permission," he told reporters. "This is not an issue on which they have a vote."
Some U.S. allies including Britain, Germany, Canada and Japan expressed general support for the raid. But others including France withheld such backing and Russia denounced the military inititiative.
"Russia insists that all military actions in Iraq threatening its sovereignty ... are stopped," the Itar-Tass news agency quoted a government statement as saying.

The move also intruded into U.S. politics. Clinton's presidential election opponent, Republican Bob Dole, said he supported the American military forces involved but made clear he blamed Clinton's "weak" policies for the situation.
